title: PRISM: A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Programmatic Spatial Reasoning
claim: A broad, diverse benchmark spanning many subject areas exposes consistent weaknesses across leading models on several complementary metrics.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right: radial subject wheel with examples, then radar chart
description: The left panel is a circular, watercolor-style wheel around a central glass prism. Its sectors are subject categories: Philosophy, Literature, Economics & Management, Physics, Electronic Information, Mathematics, Computer Science and Others. Each sector has pastel tiles radiating outward. Around the wheel sit colored question prompts, such as a Bayesian network definition or error-correcting codes. Each prompt has a dark thumbnail of a generated animation slide. The right panel is a radar chart with six axes: Executability, PADVC, In-Bound, Containment, Separation and TD. Overlapping translucent polygons compare seven LLMs, with a legend of logos and line markers below. The eye goes first to the colorful wheel, then to the blue radar polygons.
caption: Qualitative contrast between pixel-level and programmatic video generation.
abstract: Programmatic video generation through code offers geometric precision and temporal coherence beyond pixel-level diffusion models, yet rigorously evaluating whether language models can maintain spatially correct layouts throughout evolving animation sequences remains an open problem. We introduce **PRISM**, a large-scale benchmark for long-horizon programmatic spatial reasoning comprising 10,372 human-calibrated instruction-code pairs ($20\times$ larger than prior programmatic video generation benchmarks), grounded in real-world knowledge visualization scenarios across English and Chinese and spanning 437 subject categories. We further propose a funnel-style evaluation framework with four complementary metrics: *Code-Level Reliability* for executability, *Spatial Reasoning* for layout correctness over full animation sequences, and *Prompt-Aware Dynamic Visual Complexity* (PADVC) and *Temporal Density* (TD) for diagnosing dynamic expression and temporal activity. Systematic evaluation of seven mainstream LLMs reveals a striking *Execution-Spatial Gap*: the average drop from execution success rate to spatial pass rate is approximately 41 percentage points, showing that runnable code does not necessarily yield spatially coherent visual output. These findings motivate evaluation beyond executability and establish PRISM as a benchmark for spatially coherent code generation.
